reason: E1 and E2 provide direct evidence that dislocation glide destroys SRO in CrCoNi, leading to rejuvenation and lower stacking-fault energy, which supports premises 1–3. E3 shows that interfaces control creep in high-entropy superalloys, supporting premise 4. However, no cited evidence addresses the selective alteration of interfacial SRO in FCC/BCC multilayers (premise 5), and the transfer of SRO-mediated rejuvenation to creep in nanoscale multilayers is not directly supported.
premises: Dislocation glide destroys SRO, creating a rejuvenated higher-energy state with lower stacking-fault energy
SRO breakdown/rejuvenation enhances ductility and promotes localized deformation (e.g., stacking faults, shear bands)
SRO evolution can be triggered by sustained mechanical loading and controls deformation behavior
Interfaces (e.g., γ/γ′) strongly block dislocation motion and control creep resistance in high-entropy systems
SRO can be selectively altered at interfaces without unintended microstructural changes
